blocks.text: 14.3.3 Substation Bundles and Outage Coordination
The ten-year plan reached the operations team, who schedule the outages, and came back with two comments:

**Request 3.** A transformer can only be swapped with its substation out of service. Each outage costs about $300k (switching, a mobile substation, overtime), whether we swap one unit or five, so units at one substation should be done together. And the system operator allows each region at most two planned substation outages a year. The plan must pay for its outages from the same budget and stay within the operator's limit.
The code before this lesson is snapshot `steps/02`; after it, `steps/03`. The fleet is the invented 500-unit one.
The Ten-Year Model Prices Units, Not Outages, So Its Plan Breaks Both Rules
The model of the last lesson has one variable per unit and year and a budget row that adds up unit costs. An outage appears nowhere. `bundles.py` takes that plan and counts what it would really cost:
ten-year plan, costed : 161 units, 137 outages (1.18 units each), years over budget 10, most outages in a region-year 9

137 outages for 161 units: the plan almost never puts two units of one substation in the same year, because nothing told it that doing so saves anything. Costed at $300k each, every one of the ten years goes over budget, and one region takes nine outages in a year where the operator allows two. The plan is not a plan.

No coefficient change can fix this. An outage's cost is shared by every unit at the substation that year: it is paid once if any of them is replaced, and once only. That is a **fixed charge**, and a fixed charge needs a variable of its own, linked to the others by an implication (lesson 6.1.2).

Adding $300k to every unit's cost $`c_i`$ is the obvious coefficient change, and it shows why. The budget row stays linear, the model gains no variable and no row, and the money lands in the budget row, where $`c_i`$ already is. It is wrong for one reason: it charges two units at one substation for two outages in a year where they share one.
An Outage Is a Binary per Substation and Year, Linked to the Units It Serves
The new decision is $`o_{s,t} \in \{0,1\}`$: substation $`s`$ is out of service in year $`t`$. Three rules use it:

items: **No replacement without its outage.** If any unit of substation $`s`$ is replaced in year $`t`$, then $`o_{s,t} = 1`$.
**The budget pays for outages:** each year's spend is its units' costs plus $`F`$ per outage.
**Coordination:** each region has at most $`O`$ outages a year.

blocks.text: Rules 2 and 3 are rows on sums of $`o`$. Rule 1, the link, has two standard forms, and choosing between them is this lesson's design decision:

Here $`I_s`$ is the set of candidates at substation $`s`$ and $`n_s = |I_s|`$ their number. Both forms allow exactly the same 0-1 plans: with $`o_{s,t} = 0`$ both force every $`x_{i,t}`$ at $`s`$ to 0, and with $`o_{s,t} = 1`$ both allow any of them. The aggregated form is the one engineers write first, because it is one row per substation and year, where the per-unit form has one per unit and year. The project takes it, for now, and leaves a note: the two forms differ in their LP relaxation (lesson 6.7.1), and if the model gets slow at scale, this is the first place to look. A later lesson of this module comes back to it.

A third option was considered and rejected: a variable per *bundle*, "replace this set of units at this substation in this year", one for each subset. It states the rule exactly and needs no link, but a substation of 14 candidates has $`2^{14}`$ subsets. That is column generation's territory (lesson 11.3.4), not this project's.
The Model
The ten-year model with outages. Changes from the last lesson are marked.

**Sets.** $`I`$, the candidates (age 40 or more); $`Y`$, the plan years 2027–2036; $`W`$, the 20-year risk window; $`S`$, the substations with at least one candidate $`\leftarrow`$; $`I_s \subseteq I`$, the candidates at substation $`s`$ $`\leftarrow`$; $`G`$, the regions, and $`S_g \subseteq S`$ the substations of region $`g`$ $`\leftarrow`$.

**Parameters.** $`\text{rr}_{i,t}`$, discounted risk removed ($k); $`c_i`$, replacement cost ($k); $`B`$, budget per year ($k); $`F`$, the cost of one substation outage ($k) $`\leftarrow`$; $`O`$, the most outages a region may have in a year $`\leftarrow`$; $`n_s = |I_s|`$ $`\leftarrow`$.

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0,1\}`$ for $`i \in I`$, $`t \in Y`$: unit $`i`$ is replaced in year $`t`$; $`o_{s,t} \in \{0,1\}`$ for $`s \in S`$, $`t \in Y`$: substation $`s`$ has an outage in year $`t`$ $`\leftarrow`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{t \in Y} \text{rr}_{i,t} \, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

The objective does not price outages: their cost is in the budget row, where it competes with replacements for the same money, which is what operations asked for. In the code the rows are `outage_S0007_2029`, `coord_north_2029` and `budget_2029`, and the outage variables `out_S0007_2029`.
The Change, File by File

**`request.py`: two fields become real.** `outage_cost` is $`F`$ and `outages` is $`O`$, with `None` for "no limit". The defaults (0 and `None`) leave the model of the last lesson unchanged, and `has_outages` says whether the outage variables are needed at all. Three stubs belong to the next lesson.

--- 02/renewal/request.py
+++ 03/renewal/request.py
@@
-from dataclasses import dataclass
+from dataclasses import dataclass, field

 from .fleet import FIRST_YEAR
@@
     rate: float = 0.07          # discount rate for risk removed in later years
     min_age: int = 0            # units younger than this, in FIRST_YEAR, are not candidates
     gap: float = 0.0            # stop when the plan is within this share of the bound
+    outage_cost: int = 0        # $k for each substation taken out of service in a year
+    outages: int | None = None  # most substation outages per region per year; None: no limit
     # Stubs: the next lesson gives these fields their meaning; this model ignores them.
-    outage_cost: int = 0
-    outages: int | None = None
+    crew_weeks: int | None = None
+    lead_times: bool = False
+    spares: dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=dict)
+
+    def has_outages(self) -> bool:
+        return self.outage_cost > 0 or self.outages is not None

**`model.py`: outage variables, two row families, and a budget row that pays for outages.** `Built` gains `out`, the outage variables by `(substation, year)`, with an empty default so that every old caller still works, and `build` hands it over at the end:

--- 02/renewal/model.py
+++ 03/renewal/model.py
@@
-from dataclasses import dataclass
+from dataclasses import dataclass, field

 from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt

-from .fleet import Transformer
+from .fleet import REGIONS, Transformer
 from .request import Request
 from .risk import risk_removed
@@
     budget: dict[int, mathopt.LinearConstraint]     # one row per year
+    out: dict[tuple[str, int], mathopt.Variable] = field(default_factory=dict)   # out[s, t] = 1: outage
@@
     model.maximize(sum(risk_removed(t, y, request) * x[t.tid, y] for t in units for y in years))
-    return Built(model, x, budget)
+    return Built(model, x, budget, out)

Between the variables and the objective, the last lesson's `budget` comprehension gives way to the three blocks this lesson adds, and they are yours to write in the practice. Each is one line of the model above:

items: **The outage variables.** Only when `request.has_outages()`; otherwise `out` stays an empty dict and the model is the last lesson's. Then one binary $`o_{s,t}`$ for each substation $`s`$ with at least one candidate (`t.substation`, in sorted order) and each plan year, named `out_<s>_<year>` and kept in `out` under the key `(s, year)`.

**$`\text{outage}_{s,t}`$.** For each of those substations and years, the sum of $`x_{i,t}`$ over the substation's candidates at most their count $`n_s`$ times $`o_{s,t}`$, named `outage_<s>_<year>`. With $`o_{s,t} = 0`$ the row forces every one of those $`x_{i,t}`$ to 0; with $`o_{s,t} = 1`$ it allows all of them, which is why the coefficient is $`n_s`$ and not 1.

**$`\text{coord}_{g,t}`$.** Only when `request.outages` is not `None`. For each region in `REGIONS` and each plan year, the sum of $`o_{s,t}`$ over the region's substations with candidates at most `request.outages`, named `coord_<region>_<year>`. Skip a region with no candidate substations: its sum would be an empty sum, the number 0, which MathOpt refuses as a row.

**$`\text{budget}_t`$, changed.** Each year's row is the last lesson's sum of $`c_i \, x_{i,t}`$ plus `request.outage_cost` times the sum of that year's $`o_{s,t}`$, still at most `request.budget` and still named `budget_<year>`. With no outages the added term is zero.

blocks.text: Write them plainly, scanning the candidates where you need a substation's or a region's members: on 211 candidates that costs nothing anyone could measure. It is the kind of line a fleet ten times larger finds, and the scale lesson of this module measures it.
**`report.py`: outages in the money.** `outages` lists the substation-years a plan needs, one per substation and year however many units, and `spend_by_year` charges each once:
This is the report's own count, written apart from the model, so a test can compare the two.
Pricing the Outage Bundles the Work; the Region Limit Then Spreads It
`bundles.py` solves the 500-unit fleet three ways: the ten-year plan costed afterwards (above), the outage cost alone, and the cost with the limit of two outages per region and year:

ten-year plan, costed : 161 units, 137 outages (1.18 units each), years over budget 10, most outages in a region-year 9
outage cost only      : 144 units,  62 outages (2.32 units each), years over budget 0, most outages in a region-year 4
cost and region limit : 140 units,  59 outages (2.37 units each), years over budget 0, most outages in a region-year 2
ten-year plan         : risk removed $523,787k (bound $528,226k, OPTIMAL)
outage cost only      : risk removed $464,438k (bound $471,541k, OPTIMAL)
cost and region limit : risk removed $464,155k (bound $471,135k, OPTIMAL)

With outages priced, the plan replaces 144 units in 62 outages, about twice as many units per outage, and every year fits its budget. It replaces 17 fewer units, because $18,600k of the ten years' money now pays for outages. The region limit then brings the busiest region-year from four outages to two.

The last two values differ by $283k, and that difference means nothing. Each run stops within 2% of its bound, and 2% of $471,000k is about $9,400k: the solver may have stopped at either plan's value with a better one left unfound. All the runs can say is that the limit costs at most $7,386k (the bound without the limit, $471,541k, less the plan with it, $464,155k), and possibly nothing. A comparison between two runs is only as fine as the looser of their gaps, a point a later lesson of this module returns to.
The Tests Pin the Fixed Charge, the Bundle, the Region Limit and the Report
Each test builds two or three units at one or two substations:

items: **one outage serves every unit at its substation that year:** two $400k units at S1 plus one outage is $1,100k and fits a $1,100k budget; one unit at S1 and one at S2 needs two outages, $1,400k, and is refused.
**the plan bundles:** A and B at S1, C at S2, all $300k with equal risk, $900k a year and $300k outages: the plan must take A and B (one outage), not A and C (two).
**a region takes a limited number of outages a year:** with a limit of one, S1 in 2027 and S2 in 2028 is allowed; both in 2027 is refused; a third substation in another region is not affected.
**spend counts each outage once**, in the report's own arithmetic.

What the Step Did to the Code

Thirty code lines, and `build` is now the most branching function in the project, at 13: two `if`s guard optional rules, four loops walk substations, regions and years, and the comprehensions filter by substation and region. The model keeps its style (one block per constraint family, each named as in the formulation), but `build` is now long enough that the next rule should not simply be appended to it. The project lets it grow for one more lesson and then restructures it, when there is a measured reason to.

**Practice.** This lesson's project practice starts from the code before this step, the whole package (snapshot `steps/02`). It is graded by the tests in the practice's `tests/` folder and by a check that `main.py` prints the practice's `expected/report.txt`; the practice's statement gives the request `main.py` makes and the format of every line it prints. This step's `main.py` plans a tiny fleet of 25 units, drawn from seed 56, over five years, with outages.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Summary

items: **A cost shared by several decisions is a fixed charge, and needs its own variable.** No coefficient on $`x`$ can say "paid once if any unit at the substation is replaced".
**The link has two forms that allow the same 0-1 plans:** one aggregated row per substation and year, or one row per unit and year. The project starts with the smaller, aggregated one.
**Pricing outages bundled the work** (1.18 to 2.32 units per outage) and brought every year within budget; the region limit then spread the outages.
**Two runs differ meaningfully only by more than their gaps.** Within a 2% gap, $283k of difference is noise.

Both were read from the copy installed in the course's runner image. Lessons 6.1.2 (implication as a linear row), 6.7.1 (comparing formulations by their LP bound) and 11.3.4 (column generation) are the course's background for this step.
Challenges

items: Operations says a substation may have at most one planned outage in the whole ten years. Write the row, and predict whether the number of units per outage rises.
The outage cost depends on the substation: $500k where a mobile substation must be hired, $200k elsewhere. Which parameter becomes indexed, and which line of `build` changes?
Write a test that a plan with no replacements at a substation never pays for its outage. Does the model need a row for that, or does the objective take care of it?

blocks.text: Design Note: The Cost Lives in the Budget Row, Not the Objective

The outage cost could have been subtracted in the objective instead, as a price on $`o_{s,t}`$. Operations' request was about money from the same budget, so the cost goes where the money is. In the objective it would have traded risk against dollars at an exchange rate nobody had agreed on, and the plan could have spent its whole budget on units and still paid for outages on paper.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**bundles.py.** Costs the ten-year plan's outages, solves with the outage cost and then with the region limit too, and runs the step's tests before and after the change (*every section*). *Try:* Raise the outage cost to $600k. Predict the number of units per outage, then run it.
